items.text:
**Yes. Your development plan depends on ongoing AI oversight of the rules engine—not just help writing the initial code.** My previous answer understated that dependence.

Telling you that you should eventually be able to independently understand and audit every interaction would effectively require you to acquire much of the engineering expertise you are using AI to compensate for. **That should not be a prerequisite for making your game.**

You are asking AI to supply part of the development and testing capacity that you do not otherwise have. That includes interpreting approved rules, tracing interactions, finding contradictions, implementing behavior, investigating failures, and maintaining regression tests. Writing C# is only one part of that job.

## The responsibility split should reflect that

**You remain the design authority.** You decide what a mechanic is supposed to accomplish, resolve genuine design choices, approve departures from existing rules, and judge whether playing the result feels right. You should receive understandable explanations of consequential changes.

**AI provides ongoing engineering and review assistance.** I would assign it responsibility for tracing affected systems, proposing implementations, constructing tests, examining failures, and explaining where the evidence is incomplete. That is a continuing role throughout development and maintenance—not something we assume disappears once the first build works.

**The project preserves the evidence.** Approved rules, worked examples, implementation references, unresolved decisions, and test results should live in the repository. We should not depend on a particular conversation remembering everything correctly.

That last part is especially important: **the next AI session should be able to reconstruct why something works the way it does without inventing the missing history.**

## AI can build the oversight tools, too

You should not have to manually inspect thousands of interactions to determine whether a change is safe.

For example, suppose we change how an effect expires. The development workflow should produce a report along these lines:

> This change affects expiration timing and three dependent interactions. The approved examples still pass. One additional scenario fails because an effect remains active after its removal event. Here is the failing sequence and the proposed correction.

That is something you can evaluate as the game’s designer without personally reading every line involved.

AI can help write and maintain those tests. The important safeguard is that their expected outcomes come from **approved rules and independently specified examples**, rather than simply declaring whatever the implementation currently does to be correct. An AI review is a useful judgment; an executable test gives us a repeatable check. Neither makes the other unnecessary.

This dependence also does not automatically require a live AI model to adjudicate every combat turn. We can rely heavily on AI to develop and oversee a rules engine whose actual gameplay resolution is explicit code.

**The realistic goal is not “Chris becomes capable of maintaining the entire game without AI.” It is “Chris can direct, evaluate, and continue developing the game with sustained AI assistance and a project that makes errors discoverable.”**

That is the development model I should have described from the beginning.
